procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated August 10, 1969, of the Calcutta High Court in Criminal Revision Nos. 238, 289 and 290 of 1969, quashing the charges framed against the accused and other proceedings based thereon in case No. C/3443 of 1967.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The 4th accused moved the High Court in Criminal Revision No. 238 of 1969 for quashing the charges and proceedings before the Magistrate. There was an alternative prayer for stay of criminal proceedings pending the disposal of Civil Suit No. 2283. The High Court heard Criminal Revisions 238, 289, and 290 together and issued a common judgment. The High Court quashed the charges framed against the accused.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The complainant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's judgment and order, and directed the Presidency Magistrate to proceed with the trial expeditiously.

directions: The judgment and order of the High Court quashing the charges framed against the accused as well as the other proceedings based thereon, pending in case No. C/3443 of 1967, are set aside.
The learned Presidency Magistrate will proceed with the further trial and give it a very expeditious disposal.

The directions given by the Chief Presidency Magistrate regarding the examination of two more prosecution witnesses and the court witness will stand, subject to any modifications that may be made by that Court in regard to the directions already given by it.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising its jurisdiction under Section 439 of the Criminal Procedure Code to quash the charges and proceedings in the absence of a glaring defect in procedure, a manifest error of law, or a flagrant miscarriage of justice.

facts: The High Court quashed criminal charges and proceedings against the accused at a very late stage of the trial.
By the time the accused approached the High Court, charges had already been framed, several prosecution witnesses had been examined and cross-examined, and documentary evidence had been submitted.

The High Court's reasons for quashing the proceedings included its belief that the complainant had suppressed facts and its own assessment that the evidence on record did not establish an offense of breach of trust.
law: The jurisdiction of a High Court under Section 439 of the Criminal Procedure Code to quash proceedings is to be exercised only in exceptional cases.
The conditions for such interference are the presence of a glaring defect in procedure, a manifest error of law, and a consequent flagrant miscarriage of justice.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had not identified any of the required exceptional circumstances (glaring defect, manifest error of law, or miscarriage of justice) to warrant its interference.
The Court criticized the High Court for intervening at such a late stage, stating that the proper course would have been to allow the trial to reach its logical conclusion.

The Supreme Court held that the High Court should not have undertaken an appreciation of the evidence. It ruled that determining whether facts were suppressed or if the evidence established an offense was the role of the Trial Magistrate, who had to consider the entire case, not the High Court at an intermediate stage.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in quashing the charges and proceedings. It found that the necessary legal conditions for exercising its jurisdiction under Section 439 were absent, and the High Court had improperly interfered with the trial process. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and directed the trial to continue.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, at an interlocutory stage, should undertake an appreciation of evidence to determine if an offence of breach of trust has been committed.

facts: The High Court was asked to quash criminal proceedings for breach of trust at a late stage, when the trial was almost complete.
The High Court reviewed the evidence that had been presented so far in the trial.

Based on its own "appreciation of the evidence", the High Court concluded that the evidence on record did not establish an offence of breach of trust and consequently quashed the charges and proceedings.
law: The question of whether the evidence on record establishes an offence is a matter for the Trial Court to decide.
A higher court, at an interlocutory stage (i.e., before the trial is complete), should not undertake an appreciation of the evidence to determine the merits of the case.
The Trial Court must come to a conclusion after appraising the entire evidence presented by both the prosecution and the defence.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court acted improperly by engaging in a "fairly elaborate appreciation of the evidence" to decide if a breach of trust had occurred.

The Court pointed out that the High Court had contradicted itself; it had correctly declined to evaluate the evidence on one issue but then incorrectly proceeded to do so on another, more substantive issue.
The Supreme Court explicitly stated that the High Court was "not justified at that stage to have embarked upon an appreciation of the evidence."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was in error. The task of appreciating the evidence to determine whether an offence of breach of trust has been committed is the responsibility of the Trial Court after all evidence has been presented, not the High Court at an interlocutory stage.

issue.issue_text: Whether the alleged suppression of materials in a complaint is a sufficient ground for the High Court to quash the proceedings, or if it is a matter to be considered by the Trial Court.

facts: The accused argued before the High Court that the complainant had suppressed material facts in the complaint, which vitiated the proceedings.
The High Court accepted this contention and, on this basis, quashed the charges and the entire proceedings against the accused.
law: The question of whether a complainant has suppressed material facts is a matter of evidence and fact-finding.
The appropriate forum to consider and decide upon allegations of suppression of facts is the Trial Court, not the High Court in a quashing petition.
application: The Supreme Court stated that it would not express an opinion on whether there was suppression.
It reasoned that even assuming suppression had occurred, it was a matter for the Trial Magistrate to consider after appraising all the evidence from both the prosecution and the defense.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court was not justified in embarking upon an appreciation of evidence at that stage to determine if facts were suppressed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the alleged suppression of materials in a complaint is not a sufficient ground for the High Court to quash proceedings. It held that this is a matter to be considered and decided by the Trial Court during the trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising its jurisdiction under Section 439 of the Criminal Procedure Code to quash the charges and proceedings in the absence of a glaring defect in procedure, a manifest error of law, or a flagrant miscarriage of justice.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (supported by the State) argued that the High Court was not justified in quashing the charges and the entire proceedings.
The High Court should not have interfered, especially since the trial had been ongoing for a considerable time and was nearing its conclusion.

The accused did not approach the High Court at the earliest possible stage (e.g., when summons were issued or charges were framed), which they should have done if they believed the proceedings should be quashed.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (accused) argued that the High Court was justified in quashing the charge and the entire proceedings based on the circumstances of the case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, at an interlocutory stage, should undertake an appreciation of evidence to determine if an offence of breach of trust has been committed.
appellant_arguments: The High Court should not have embarked upon an appreciation of evidence at this stage.
Whether the evidence on record establishes an offence is a matter for the Trial Court to decide after all evidence from both the prosecution and defence has been presented.

The High Court was inconsistent, as it rightly declined to appreciate evidence for one of the respondent's contentions (the third) but then wrongly engaged in a detailed appreciation of evidence for another (the fifth).
respondent_arguments: The respondent's fifth contention, which the High Court accepted, was that the merits of the case, based on the oral and documentary evidence on record, should be considered.
The respondent argued that the evidence on record ruled out the possibility of any offence of breach of trust being committed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the alleged suppression of materials in a complaint is a sufficient ground for the High Court to quash the proceedings, or if it is a matter to be considered by the Trial Court.
appellant_arguments: The alleged suppression of materials is not a valid ground for the High Court to quash the proceedings at this stage.
Even if there was suppression, it is a matter to be considered by the Trial Magistrate during the course of the trial.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's fourth contention, which the High Court accepted, was that there was a suppression of material facts by the complainant, which justified quashing the proceedings.

cases.case_name: R. K. Kapur v. The Stare of Punjab
cases.principle: To establish the principles for exercising inherent jurisdiction under s. 561A, Cr. P. C. to quash proceedings.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The High Court's jurisdiction to interfere with ongoing proceedings under section 439 of the Criminal Procedure Code is to be exercised only in exceptional cases where there is a glaring defect in procedure, a manifest error on a point of law, and a consequent flagrant miscarriage of justice.
obiter: The High Court should not, at an interlocutory stage, undertake an appreciation of evidence to determine a question of fact, as that is a matter for the trial court to assess and decide after all evidence is presented.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was in error for quashing the charges and proceedings. The High Court's jurisdiction under Section 439 of the Criminal Procedure Code is to be exercised only in exceptional cases where there is a glaring defect in procedure, a manifest error of law, or a flagrant miscarriage of justice. The Supreme Court found that the High Court did not identify any of these circumstances and improperly interfered by undertaking an appreciation of evidence on the merits, a function that belongs to the trial court, especially when the trial was already at an advanced stage.
legal_tests_applied: The jurisdiction of the High Court is to be exercised normally, under the section [439 Cr.P.C.], only in exceptional. cases when there is a glaring defect in the procedure or there is a manifest error on a point of law and consequently a flagrant mis-carriage of justice.
why_appellant_lost: The High Court's decision to quash the proceedings was based on its acceptance of the accused's fourth contention, which alleged a suppression of material facts by the complainant.

The High Court's decision was also based on its acceptance of the accused's fifth contention, which involved an assessment of the merits of the case based on the evidence on record, leading the High Court to conclude that the evidence ruled out any offence of breach of trust.
why_respondent_won: The High Court accepted the respondent's argument that there was a suppression of material facts by the complainant, which justified quashing the proceedings.

The High Court engaged in an appreciation of the evidence on record at an interlocutory stage and concluded, in favor of the respondent, that the evidence 'rules out any offence of breach of trust or a conspiracy to commit the same, by the accused persons'.
policy_considerations: The High Court's revisional jurisdiction should not be used to interfere with ongoing trial proceedings at a late stage, especially when the trial is nearing its logical conclusion.

A higher court should not usurp the function of the trial court by conducting a premature appreciation of evidence to determine the merits of a case; that assessment should be made by the trial magistrate after all evidence has been presented.
